extracted.intended_audience: general readers and mathematicians interested in mathematics, aesthetics, and science writing
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or composing popular-science/essay pieces about mathematical beauty, distinguishing types of aesthetic appeal and how a piece succeeds by emphasizing one or the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic Beauty (the "Cold and Formal")
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty that is ethereal, formal, reflecting abstract structures and patterns — a universal order and logical sequences; values abstraction and general principles applicable to entire categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for emphasis on broad, unifying structures (e.g., natural numbers, Euclidean spaces, formal logic). Praise language that highlights universality, elegance of general principles, logical simplicity, and how a concept organizes many cases. Appropriate for pieces that aim to show why a mathematical idea has wide explanatory or conceptual reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptional Beauty (the "Curiosity Cabinet")
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty focused on outliers and one-of-a-kind objects; relatable, exotic, intimate, and subjective — celebrating curiosities that don't fit larger patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for attention to singular, striking examples (e.g., the dodecahedron, the Monster group). Effective exposition makes the object feel vivid and special — 'complicated, but not too complicated' — and appeals to personal fascination. Suitable for pieces that aim to charm or intrigue by zooming in on particular mathematical marvels rather than general theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether the piece captures a general structural pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: A criterion for judging if the writing successfully Presents a general, unifying structural insight rather than an isolated curiosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the piece explains principles that apply broadly, clarifies how the structure organizes many phenomena, and communicates why the abstraction matters. Examples and historical context that show broad applicability strengthen this axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether the piece illuminates a singular striking object
rubrics_metrics.description: A criterion for judging if the writing successfully highlights a unique, attention-grabbing mathematical object and makes it compelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess narrative vividness, relatability, and the ability to convey why the object is remarkable. Use concrete description and storytelling to make the singularity meaningful without forcing unjustified generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate the two registers
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid collapsing generic and exceptional beauty into one indistinct notion; they are different tastes and serve different rhetorical and epistemic goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or evaluating, be explicit about which register is intended. Critiques should respect that a piece may succeed on one axis (e.g., charm of a curiosity) even if it fails on the other (e.g., broad explanatory power). Conflation is an anti-pattern that obscures real distinctions in mathematician taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical-explanatory power favors generic beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical and epistemic claim that generic (abstract) beauty has proven more powerful for understanding the physical universe than exceptional, singular beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims about relevance to physics or natural phenomena, give weight to demonstrations that a mathematical structure yields broad explanatory success (e.g., Newton's abstract law vs. Kepler's focus on Platonic solids). Use historical examples to judge whether the mathematical idea maps onto physical regularities.
